questions.q:
These two instructions run in order:

mov rax, 5
mov rbx, rax

What do RAX and RBX hold afterwards?
choices: RAX = 5, RBX = 5
RAX = 0, RBX = 5
RAX = 5, RBX = 0
RAX = 0, RBX = 0
questions.explain: MOV copies. The first instruction puts 5 in RAX. The second copies RAX into RBX, and RAX keeps its 5.

questions.q: After `mov rbx, rax`, the value is gone from RAX because it was moved into RBX.
questions.explain: Despite the name, MOV is a copy. The source register still holds its value.

questions.q: In the instruction `mov rbx, rax`, which operand is the destination?
choices: rbx, the first operand
rax, the second operand
Both: the values are swapped
Neither: the result goes to the instruction pointer
questions.explain: In this syntax the form is `mov destination, source`, so this reads as 'move into RBX the value in RAX'.

questions.q: Write one instruction that copies the value in RAX into RBX.
questions.explain: Write `mov`, then the destination register, a comma, and the source: `mov rbx, rax`.

questions.q: After `mov rcx, 0x1234`, what value does RCX hold, written in decimal?
questions.explain: 0x1234 = 1*4096 + 2*256 + 3*16 + 4 = 4096 + 512 + 48 + 4 = 4660. The immediate is written in hex but it is the same number.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a valid use of MOV?
choices: Putting an immediate decimal value in a register
Putting an immediate hex value in a register
Copying one general-purpose register into another
Loading a value from a memory address into a register
Writing a value straight into RIP
questions.explain: MOV can take immediates (decimal or hex), registers, and memory loads. RIP cannot be a MOV destination, and the assembler rejects it.

questions.q: Why are values in assembly so often written in hexadecimal?
choices: Hex converts easily to other representations, binary in particular
The CPU can only store hex values
Decimal immediates are a syntax error
Hex values run faster than decimal ones
questions.explain: Each hex digit maps to exactly 4 bits, so hex is easy to convert to binary. Decimal immediates such as `mov rax, 5` are still allowed.

questions.q: In the GNU assembler syntax used here, which of these lines are comments?
choices: # this is a comment
/* this is a comment */
; this is a comment
-- this is a comment
% this is a comment
questions.explain: This assembler accepts a pound sign (#) or a C-style /* ... */ comment. Other assemblers and architectures use other symbols, so comment syntax is not universal.

questions.q: A C-style comment such as /* note */ can go in the middle of a line of code.
questions.explain: The /* ... */ form has an explicit end marker, so it can sit inside a line and the instruction still assembles and runs.

questions.q: The leading zeros in a memory address are required: `[0x00401000]` works but `[0x401000]` does not.
questions.explain: Leading zeros are optional. Both refer to the same address.

questions.q: What do the square brackets do in `mov rdx, [0x401000]`?
choices: They make MOV go to address 0x401000 in memory and load what is stored there
They load the number 0x401000 itself into RDX
They write RDX's value to address 0x401000
They mark 0x401000 as a comment
questions.explain: Brackets mean the operand is a memory address to look up. MOV goes to that address and brings back the contents instead of using the number itself.

questions.q: What is the difference between `mov rdx, 0x401000` and `mov rdx, [0x401000]`?
choices: The first puts the number 0x401000 in RDX. The second puts the data stored at address 0x401000 in RDX.
They do exactly the same thing
The first reads memory and the second uses an immediate value
The second writes RDX to memory
questions.explain: Without brackets the operand is an immediate value. With brackets it is an address, and MOV loads the data stored there.

questions.q: How many bytes does `mov rdx, [address]` read from memory, given that RDX is a 64-bit register?
questions.explain: A 64-bit register holds 8 bytes, so the load reads 8 bytes starting at that address.

questions.q: When bytes are loaded from memory into a register, they appear in the register in the same order they sit in memory, reading left to right.
questions.explain: They come out backwards. The byte at the lowest address ends up at the right-hand (least significant) end of the register's value.

questions.q:
Starting at address 0x401000, memory holds these bytes, lowest address first:

48 C7 C0 05 00 00 00 48

What value is in RDX after `mov rdx, [0x401000]`?
questions.explain: All 8 bytes are loaded and they appear backwards. The first byte (48) ends up on the right, and the last byte (48) ends up on the left: 0x4800000005C0C748.

questions.q: The bytes at 0x401000 are the 7-byte machine code for `mov rax, 5` (48 C7 C0 05 00 00 00), followed by the next instruction. Why does `mov rdx, [0x401000]` also pick up the first byte of the next instruction?
choices: The load reads 8 bytes to fill the 64-bit register, and the first instruction is only 7 bytes long
MOV always reads one extra byte as a checksum
The instruction pointer adds the next byte automatically
The brackets make MOV read until it reaches a zero byte
questions.explain: A load into a 64-bit register reads 8 bytes no matter where instructions begin or end. Seven bytes belong to `mov rax, 5`, so the eighth comes from the next instruction.

questions.q: What does the instruction pointer (RIP) hold?
choices: The address of the next instruction to execute, which the CPU uses to track its place
The result of the most recent MOV
The address of the top of the stack
A count of how many instructions have run
questions.explain: RIP points to where execution is. It updates on its own and steps forward through the code with each instruction.

questions.q: What happens when you try to assemble `mov rip, 0x401000`?
choices: The assembler rejects it with an 'operand type mismatch for mov' error
RIP is set and execution jumps to 0x401000
It assembles, but RIP ignores the write
It assembles into a comment
questions.explain: RIP is protected and cannot be a MOV destination. The assembler reports an operand type mismatch.

questions.q: If MOV cannot write to RIP, how does a program change where execution goes?
choices: With dedicated control-flow instructions that modify RIP
By copying the new address into RSP
By putting the address in a comment
There is no way. Execution can only go forward.
questions.explain: Other instructions exist to modify RIP, and they are how control flow works. A plain MOV into RIP is not allowed.

questions.q: Which registers should you avoid writing to unless you are doing it deliberately for a specific reason?
choices: RSP (stack pointer)
RBP (base pointer)
RIP (instruction pointer)
RAX
RCX
questions.explain: RSP and RBP belong to the stack, and RIP controls execution (MOV can't write it at all). The others, such as RAX, RCX, and R15, are general purpose and can be written freely.

questions.q: MOV can write to the stack pointer RSP, but doing so carelessly can cause problems once real programs use the stack.
questions.explain: Unlike RIP, RSP and RBP can be written with MOV. Because they manage the stack, you should only write to them on purpose.

questions.q: When a debugger pauses a program, the highlighted instruction (the one RIP points to) has already been executed.
questions.explain: The highlighted instruction is the next one to run and has not executed yet. Stepping runs it and moves the highlight forward.

questions.q: A program contains only `mov rax, 5` and `mov rbx, rax`. Both instructions work, but the program then dies with a segmentation fault. Why?
choices: The program never exits, so execution runs past the last instruction into memory it doesn't own
MOV can't copy between two 64-bit registers
Putting 5 in RAX is illegal
Every MOV causes a segmentation fault
questions.explain: With no exit, the CPU keeps going past the code, like a car driving off a cliff. It reaches memory the program doesn't own, and the operating system reports a segmentation fault (SIGSEGV).

questions.q: What does a disassembly view show for each instruction?
choices: The memory address where the instruction lives
The raw machine code bytes, in hex
The instruction in assembly form, e.g. mov rbx, rax
How many times the instruction has run
questions.explain: Each entry shows the instruction's address, its machine code in hex, and the matching assembly instruction.

questions.q: Assembly instructions go through an intermediary compiler that may change them before the CPU executes them.
questions.explain: The assembler translates assembly instructions directly into the machine instructions the CPU executes, with no intermediary compiler.
